title: Peptic Ulcer Disease - Epigastric Pain with Incidental Gallstones on Ultrasound
patient_instructions: You are David Nguyen, a 40-year-old man attending a general practice with ongoing pain in the upper-middle part of your stomach (epigastric). The pain has been continuous for a few weeks, staying the same rather than getting worse, and it gets WORSE when you eat - especially chilli and spicy food. Antacids (like Mylanta) make it BETTER; volunteer this only if asked what helps. You take ibuprofen regularly for chronic lower back pain - mention this only if the candidate asks about medications. You drink 1-2 coffees a day. You recently had an ultrasound that showed gallstones, and you are worried you need your gallbladder removed. There is NO weight loss, no difficulty swallowing, no vomiting blood, no black stools, no vomiting. Ideas: you think the gallstones are causing the pain. Concerns: you are anxious about surgery. Expectations: you want to know if you need an operation. Affect: calm, mildly worried, cooperative, forthcoming when asked directly. Do not use medical terms.
candidate_instructions: You are a GP in a rural NSW practice. David Nguyen, a 40-year-old man, presents with ongoing upper abdominal pain. He brings a recent ultrasound report showing gallstones with no gallbladder inflammation and no wall thickening. Tasks: (1) Take a focused, structured history for approximately 6 minutes. (2) Explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials to the patient in plain language, addressing his concern about the gallstones. You are not required to examine the patient.
examiner_instructions: Look for a systematic history that is not short-circuited by the incidental gallstones: full pain assessment, medication history eliciting regular NSAID (ibuprofen) use, symptom pattern (worse with food/spice, relieved by antacids), and a deliberate dyspepsia alarm-feature screen (weight loss, dysphagia, haematemesis/melaena, anaemia, persistent vomiting). The expected diagnosis is peptic ulcer disease/NSAID-related dyspepsia; the gallstones are incidental. Reward candidates who separate the risk factor (NSAID) from the supporting symptom (antacid relief), and who explain WHY the gallstones are not the cause. Prompt if needed: 'What in the history are you using to weigh gallstones against other causes?' Award communication marks for reassurance and lifestyle advice.

criteria: Confirms haemodynamic stability and takes a systematic pain assessment
Elicits regular ibuprofen (NSAID) use as the key risk factor
Elicits symptom pattern: worse with food/spicy food, relieved by antacids
Completes a dyspepsia alarm-feature (red flag) screen
Does not anchor on the incidental gallstones
Identifies peptic ulcer disease / NSAID-related dyspepsia as most likely
Correctly separates NSAID as risk factor from antacid relief as a supporting feature
Lists relevant differentials including GORD, biliary colic, pancreatitis and ACS/lower-lobe pneumonia mimics
Cease/minimise NSAID and substitute paracetamol for back pain
Test for H. pylori and commence a PPI per eTG; arrange gastroscopy if red flags present
Explains incidental asymptomatic gallstones generally need no treatment
Plain-language explanation that reassures about the gallstones with reasons
Lifestyle advice (reduce alcohol/smoking/caffeine, avoid trigger foods) and checks understanding

red_flags: Dyspepsia alarm features: unintentional weight loss, dysphagia/odynophagia, haematemesis or melaena, iron-deficiency anaemia, persistent vomiting, age >50 with new symptoms, family history of upper GI cancer - any mandates gastroscopy
Regular NSAID use is a major risk factor for peptic ulceration and GI bleeding/perforation
Do not attribute symptoms to incidental gallstones and miss an NSAID-related ulcer
Epigastric pain can be a mimic of acute coronary syndrome - keep ACS in the differential
australian_guidelines: RACGP / eTG: dyspepsia alarm features mandate gastroscopy referral rather than empirical therapy
eTG (Gastrointestinal): cease/minimise NSAID, test for Helicobacter pylori (urea breath test or stool antigen) and eradicate if positive, and commence a PBS-listed PPI (e.g. esomeprazole)

Australian practice: asymptomatic (incidental) gallstones generally require no treatment; biliary colic is severe episodic post-fatty-meal RUQ/epigastric pain, distinct from constant epigastric pain relieved by antacids
RACGP patient-education / SNAP: reduce alcohol and smoking (impair ulcer healing) and moderate caffeine
learning_objectives: Take a complete dyspepsia history that is not derailed by an incidental imaging finding
Distinguish risk factors from supporting symptomatic features in clinical reasoning
Apply the Australian dyspepsia alarm-feature checklist and H. pylori / PPI management pathway
Explain to a patient why incidental gallstones are not the cause of their symptoms
key_points: Ibuprofen is the risk factor; antacid relief and food/spice aggravation are supporting features of acid-related disease
Incidental gallstones with a normal gallbladder on ultrasound do not explain constant epigastric pain relieved by antacids
First-line management: stop the NSAID, test-and-treat H. pylori, start a PPI
Keep ACS and lower-lobe pneumonia in mind as extra-abdominal mimics of upper abdominal pain

citations.claim: Upper abdominal pain differentials must include surgical emergencies such as small bowel obstruction (colicky central pain + vomiting + distension), screened in structured GI questioning.
Dyspepsia and its assessment are covered in Murtagh's General Practice, the Australian GP reference against which this PUD/dyspepsia content is consistent.
A safe diagnostic strategy with early exclusion of time-critical conditions (e.g. acute coronary events within 60-90 minutes) supports including ACS among differentials for epigastric pain.
